title: Operando Time-of-Flight Secondary Ion Mass Spectrometry Reveals Iodine-Mediated Redox Chemistry in Solid-State Li–S Batteries
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Understanding dynamic reaction pathways in all-solid-state batteries remains challenging because electrochemical processes occur at buried solid–solid interfaces and transient intermediates are difficult to detect with conventional analytical techniques. While operando techniques typically probe structural or macroscopic changes, direct detection of reactive species during operation remains experimentally demanding. Here, we introduce a dynamic operando time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry platform that enables continuous chemical analysis of processes in a solid-state battery under electrochemical bias. Using this approach, we directly observe a pronounced increase of the I2– signal during charging of a Li–S composite cathode containing LiI, indicating the formation of elemental iodine. Concurrent changes in the sulfur-containing ion signals suggest the involvement of iodine species in the ongoing redox processes. These results reveal transient, low-concentration species at buried interfaces undetectable by other operando techniques, offering a pathway for identifying reactive intermediates in conversion-type solid-state batteries and related electrochemical systems.</jats:p>
summary: A dynamic operando ToF-SIMS platform follows a solid-state Li–S cathode under bias. It detects a rising I2– signal on charging in LiI-containing cathodes, which indicates elemental iodine formation. Sulfur ion signals change at the same time, pointing to iodine-mediated redox. The work detects transient, low-concentration species at buried interfaces that other operando methods miss.

title: Quantitative Measurement of Li‐Ion Concentration in NCM811 Cathodes via Optimized Electrochemical Strain Microscopy
content:
Electrochemical strain microscopy is turned into a quantitative probe of lithium content in NCM811 cathodes. A stiff cantilever suppresses electrostatic artifacts and contact‐potential drift, and the shortened acquisition time makes multi‐particle sampling practical. The calibrated amplitude tracks bulk lithium concentration, resolving inter‐particle state‐of‐charge heterogeneity and classifying three charge states from only four images.








ABSTRACT
Inter‐particle state‐of‐charge (SOC) heterogeneity governs electrochemical degradation in Ni‐rich layered oxide cathodes, yet quantifying the underlying nanoscale lithium distribution remains inaccessible to bulk‐averaging characterization techniques and impractical for destructive nanoscale probes. Here, a practical process for nanoscale Li‐ion quantification in NCM811 cathodes is established by optimizing the measurement conditions of electrochemical strain microscopy (ESM). Through rational probe selection to suppress electrostatic artifacts and contact potential difference drift sensitivity combined with a markedly reduced acquisition time, a quantitative calibration framework directly correlating pixel‐averaged ESM amplitude with ICP‐MS‐derived bulk Li concentration is constructed. Classification among three SOCs exceeds 90% accuracy with as few as four images per sample. This work establishes multi‐particle ESM imaging as a statistically robust and non‐destructive platform for nanoscale Li‐ion quantification in NCM811 cathodes, with broad applicability across mixed ionic‐electronic conductors in which local Vegard strain arises from ion redistribution.
journal: Wiley: Small Methods: Table of Contents
summary: Turns ESM into a calibrated Li-content probe for NCM811: a stiff cantilever suppresses electrostatic and contact-potential artifacts, and faster acquisition allows multi-particle statistics. Pixel-averaged amplitude is calibrated against ICP-MS Li content, and three SOCs are classified with over 90% accuracy from four images. This is ex situ and gives only indirect quantification, but it is a useful methodological step.
technique: Electrochemical strain microscopy (AFM-based) with ICP-MS calibration

title: Layer Stacking Structure Governed Transition‐Metal Interlayer Migration for Reversible High‐Voltage Oxygen Redox Plateau
content:
A layer stacking structure governed reversible high‐voltage oxygen redox plateau is unraveled. The P2‐Na0.6Li0.2Mn0.6Ti0.2O2 with ribbon superlattice shows weak control of interlayer TM migration, which results in spontaneously molecular oxygen formation and large voltage hysteresis. The allotropic P3 stacking structure with strong control of interlayer TM migration shows reversible oxygen redox plateau.








ABSTRACT
Utilization of lattice oxygen redox electrochemistry is the holy grail for achieving high‐capacity layered cathodes. However, prior to this, the large voltage hysteresis must be overcome. In this work, we uncover a novel scientific nature of layered stacking structure‐governed interlayer transition‑metal migration that substantially modulates the reversibility of the high‐voltage oxygen plateau. It is discovered that a kind of ribbon superlattice can facilitate the reversible high‐voltage oxygen redox plateau in the P3‐Na0.6Li0.2Mn0.6Ti0.2O2 with the oxygen stacking series of “ABBCCA…”, but plays no role in the P2‐Na0.6Li0.2Mn0.6Ti0.2O2 counterpart with the oxygen stacking series of “ABBA…”. Combined with the experiments and theoretical calculations, it is unraveled that the P3 stacking framework can suppress O‐type stacking faults and in turn elevates steric hindrance to the transition metal migration and the formation of molecular oxygen, thus enabling reversible high‐voltage oxygen redox. In contrast, the P2 phase can transform into O2 phase at de‐sodiated state, which accelerates severe interlayer transition metal migration, and triggers in‐plane structural reconstruction and molecular oxygen, leading to loss of high‐voltage plateau. This finding reveals how the layer stacking structure modulates the reversible oxygen redox plateau.
journal: Wiley: Angewandte Chemie International Edition: Table of Contents
summary: Compares P2 and P3 Na0.6Li0.2Mn0.6Ti0.2O2 with the same composition. P3 stacking suppresses O-type stacking faults, which hinders interlayer TM migration and molecular O2 formation, so the high-voltage oxygen plateau stays reversible. P2 transforms to O2 stacking and loses the plateau. This is a useful structure–mechanism link, but the evidence seems to be mostly conventional diffraction, microscopy and DFT.
technique: ex situ/in situ XRD, STEM, RIXS/DFT (likely)
